t: How To Help Difficult Students Who Act Out Due To Emotional Turmoil ue-to-emotional-turmoil/
q: Many difficult students behave the way they do because they’ve experienced—and often continue to experience—emotional turmoil associated with a deplorable home life.
To reach them, your classroom must be a shelter in the midst of the storm.
It has a calming effect that makes them feel safe and valued. Done right, their shoulders will drop when they enter your classroom, their very seat becoming a refuge.
Finger-wagging lectures, dressing downs, sarcastic remarks, and other signs of taking misbehavior personally only work against you and add to their emotional pain.
Rather, with the right classroom management approach, they can begin to heal. They can begin to see themselves and their future in a different light.

t: Why Observation Should Be Your First Response To Misbehavior nse-to-misbehavior/
q: Getting involved too quickly is among the most common classroom management mistakes.
But the truth is, you’re far better off allowing misbehavior to play out.
Merely observing from a safe but noticeable distance, on the other hand, has a calming effect on students, remarkably so, and gives you a better understanding of the facts before responding.
When misbehaving students feel your heavy gaze upon them, when they know that you’re recording their every move, they’ll naturally, almost magically, take a moment’s pause.
Lessons learned on their own, you see, are lessons that resonate deep in their heart, where lasting change happens.

t: How To Rid Your Classroom Of Excitability
q: Spend a day visiting classrooms at your neighborhood school and you’ll find many buzzing with tension.
A consistently tense and excitable classroom is caused not by students, but by their teacher.
A consistently calm personality shows a leadership quality lacking in most adults students come in contact with, and they immediately respect it.
Students tend to take on the personality of their teacher. Outsiders can see this just by spending a few minutes in their company—even out of your presence.
For anxiety and stress have no place in a well-run classroom. They are saboteurs of the highest order, spawning excitability, misbehavior, unhappiness, and a teacher wound too tight to be effective.

t: How To Keep Your Students Focused The Last Hour Of The School Day t-hour-of-the-school-day/
q: So much good, quality instruction is lost in the hour before dismissal.
The truth is, the last hour of the day takes more out of you than the preceding hours put together.
In this case, ask your students to stand silently behind their desks, feet wide and hands behind their backs. Pause a moment and let their breathing regulate naturally.
It’s critically important that you finish the school day—that is, the last several minutes—without chaos, confusion, or misbehavior
Have your end-of-day routine finish with every student standing behind their desk, silent, reflective, backpack looped over shoulders.
They’ve developed the classroom management skills to keep distractions, interruptions, and time-consuming misbehaviors to a scanty, bare minimum.
